entry.title: Steben Gavino - Manabi - 70% - Caramelized Cacao Nibs

link.title: Steben Gavino - Manabi - 70% - Caramelized Cacao Nibs

entry.content:
The packaging is beautifully crafted and original, folded in origami style, with pretty designs. The bar itself is a disc with wavy edges, like a flower. This presentation is meant to reflect the prestige of Steben Gavino, an Ecuadorian named Spain’s best chocolatier in 2021

The chocolate is pleasant and refined. It melts in your mouth, releasing flavors of honey, caramel, banana, and fresh grapes. What remains are crunchy pieces of caramelized cacao, which add a hint of bitterness and nuttiness enveloped in sweetness.

It is a masterfully crafted chocolate that brings out the aromas of Manabi cacao in a well-balanced way.

Evaluation

Uniqueness: 4
Finesse: 4.5
Comfort: 4.5
Intensity: 4.5
General impression: 4.5

Final evaluation: 22/25

entry.title: Galletti - Sibarita Cocoa Pulp - 100% Cocoa
entry.content:
Here’s something interesting. Yes, it’s 100% chocolate… but it’s not what you’d think! It’s 100% cacao, but Galletti uses cacao pulp to sweeten its chocolate. It’s still cacao, right?

The experience is quite unique. The pulp adds a touch of sweetness and a tangy flavor, which blend with the astringency of pure chocolate. The result: the robust character of the original cacao is preserved, but from an original angle that remains pleasant. A successful twist.

A quick etymological note: the name “Sibarita” that Galletti gave this bar is a Spanish adjective meaning “gourmet” and “bon vivant.” It derives from the Greek city of Sybaris, which, with a population of 300,000, ruled a small empire in Calabria in 700 BCE, and whose inhabitants were known for their idleness and love of luxury. They are even said to have invented the concept of intellectual property, applied to their top priority: a chef who invented a recipe had exclusive rights to it for a year! In short, it’s a well-chosen name for a 100% chocolate bar that’s as delicious as it is original!

Evaluation

Uniqueness: 5
Finesse: 4
Comfort: 4.5
Intensity: 5
General impression: 4

Final evaluation: 22.5/25

entry.title: Pacari - Organic Chocolate with Hoja Santa - 60% Cacao

link.title: Pacari - Organic Chocolate with Hoja Santa - 60% Cacao

entry.content:
La Hoja Santa—the “holy leaf”—is a plant native to Mexico, whose flavor is described by Wikipedia as a blend of eucalyptus, licorice, nutmeg, and black pepper. It is also known as the “Leaf of Saint Mary”; both names are said to stem from its use as a support when the Virgin Mary changed the baby Jesus’s diaper. The Mexican legend provides no details regarding the location or the logistics.

In any case, I find it difficult to identify the taste of this plant. It takes a back seat to the chocolate. The influence is there, though: a pronounced herbaceous note, with a hint of mint and anise that lingers on the palate long after you’ve swallowed the piece.

Evaluation

Uniqueness: 3.5
Finesse: 4
Comfort: 4
Intensity: 4
General impression: 3.5

Final evaluation: 19/25

entry.title: Bios - Pajarito Cocoa - 70%
entry.content:
Cacao Pajarito? Little bird… It’s a pretty name. But finding out more is difficult. Bios provides no details about the bar, and there’s nothing on their website either: it’s impossible to find any mention of the bar, even though it won a gold medal at the 2024 Ecuador Chocolate Awards. A Google search doesn’t turn up much more information either. Only Noel Verde’s website mentions it: it’s said to be a rare variety of Arriba cacao.

In any case, as one says, it tastes good. Very good, in fact. It’s a rich and intense chocolate, a blend of several flavors that dance on the tongue. Round and smooth chestnut cream, tangy red berries, slightly bitter grapefruit, and comforting hazelnut take turns taking center stage in a festival of surprises. A truly wonderful experience, worthy of the finest chocolate bars.

Evaluation

Uniqueness: 5
Finesse: 5
Comfort: 4.5
Intensity: 5
General impression: 5

Final evaluation: 24.5/25

entry.title: Pacari - Galapagos Dark Shark - 75% Cacao
entry.content:
This chocolate is a mystery: on Paccari’s website, the Dark Shark Galapagos bar is described as flavored with coffee and salt. Yet the packaging makes no mention of coffee or salt, and neither flavor is detectable on the palate either.

So what exactly is this bar? A pure chocolate that clearly bears the Paccari signature in its texture and flavors. We still find it rather mild, perhaps a bit more herbal. I’m probably influenced by the name, but when I close my eyes, I feel I can sense a subtle coastal, maritime breeze that brings back certain memories of my trip to that extraordinary place.

Evaluation

Uniqueness: 4
Finesse: 4.5
Comfort: 4.5
Intensity: 4.5
General impression: 4.5

Final evaluation: 22/25

entry.title: Anquria - 63% La canela amazonica - Ishpingo
entry.content:
Ishpingo, or Mespilodaphne quixos, is a species of tree endemic to the Ecuadorian Amazon. Its bark, known as “Ecuadorian cinnamon”, has a taste similar to that of common cinnamon - produced from the bark of a tree in the same Lauraceae family (to which laurel also belongs). It’s a spice used in Ecuadorian cuisine, and Anquria tries it here with their chocolate.

The result is as original as it is delicious. Ishpingo blends with cocoa in a comforting bar reminiscent of a campfire on a summer’s night.

Evaluation

Uniqueness: 5
Finesse: 4.5
Comfort: 4.5
Intensity: 4.5
General impression: 4.5

Final evaluation: 23/25

entry.title: Kallari - Chocolate 70%
entry.content:
Light, pure, almost ethereal. Notes of vanilla, caramel and bitter almond. And a hint of that cocoa flavor that reassures us, just when we were beginning to doubt: yes, this is chocolate.

A unique bar, that bets on finesse and difference at the expense, perhaps, of the comfort we seek in chocolate.

entry.title: Hacienda San José - 80% Chocolate Negro - Los Rios

link.title: Hacienda San José - 80% Chocolate Negro - Los Rios

entry.content:
Hacienda San José comes from a line of cocoa-producing farms founded in the 1930s, during Ecuador’s cocoa boom. Renowned for its high quality cocoa beans (the best in the world! according to the text on the cover), it wasn’t until 90 years later that the owner family decided to produce its own chocolate.

Butter and hazelnut mingle with the slightly bitter, acidic notes of coffee, finishing with aromas of ripe banana. This is a chocolate that excels in the classic category - no regrets, but no surprises.

Evaluation

Uniqueness: 3.5
Finesse: 4.5
Comfort: 4.5
Intensity: 4.5
General impression: 4

Final evaluation: 21/25

entry.title: Anquria - 63% El Cacao Blanco - Macambo Caramelizado

link.title: Anquria - 63% El Cacao Blanco - Macambo Caramelizado

entry.content:
By now, you’re familiar with macambo — a cousin of cocoa that can be made into a chocolate equivalent (not as good), but can also be added in pieces to a bar, much like a nut. Here, Anquria — a new brand for me — caramelizes it beforehand, adding a touch of praline that I won’t complain about.

The chocolate itself is hard to isolate, but it leans toward the herbal and spicy: tobacco, clove, mushroom. Combined with the macambo, the result is unusual — and quietly compelling.

Evaluation

Uniqueness: 4.5
Finesse: 4.5
Comfort: 4
Intensity: 4.5
General impression: 4

Final evaluation: 21.5/25

entry.title: Wao - 70% - Cacao del Yasuni
entry.content:
Again, a chocolate from Yasuni - here, a project run by women of the Waorani community, one of the many peoples of this region of the Amazon.

This is a chocolate with an assumed power, a little raw, which begins with notes of plum liqueur and freshly cut wood, with a finish of butter and brownie. The texture, perfectly smooth, crunchy then melting, is well mastered.

An excellent chocolate.

Evaluation

Uniqueness: 4.5
Finesse: 5
Comfort: 4.5
Intensity: 4.5
General impression: 4.5

Final evaluation: 23/25
